meta.cover_subtitle: If we want to raise prices

1.title: The least bad way to raise prices
1.subtitle: Where a rise does least damage. The cost in churn is unknown.
1.notes: 3,274 subscribers affected. No free users, no annual subscribers. Our website advertises annual prices, so no public price changes.

1.title: What it raises turns on churn we can't predict
columns: If monthly churn goes from 14.9% to
1.notes: 14.9% a month is what monthly Premium customers already leave at today. Plan on 0.35 to 0.70 MSEK a year.

2.title: Why we landed on monthly plans

bullets.label: Margin
bullets.text: Plans carry almost no direct cost. Phone numbers do.

bullets.label: Headroom
bullets.text: Our plans are about 30% cheaper than Grasshopper and OpenPhone.

bullets.label: Exposure
bullets.text: 3,274 subscribers, against 23,046 who hold a US phone number.

bullets.label: Reversible
bullets.text: Everyone affected renews within a month.

2.notes: Our phone numbers already sit at the market price. Our plans do not.

2.title: The new price still undercuts the market
2.notes: Per user per month. Google Voice is cheaper but only sells inside the US. What limits us is our own customers, not the competition.

3.title: 2018–19: doubled prices, then put them back
3.notes: About a third of our customers left. We created the free plan in July 2019 in response to the exodus, not before it.

3.title: Why this time is different
left: Phone numbers, our largest revenue line
Annual and three-year prices rose too, so customers had nowhere to go but out
A quarter only met the new price at renewal, up to 36 months later
right: Annual prices unchanged, and promoted as the cheaper alternative
Everyone affected renews within a month, so we could reverse it

3.title: If we ever did raise number prices
3.subtitle: Not recommended. Kept here so the size of the prize is visible.

cells: We lost about a third of customers

3.notes: Before any customer response. Anything above $2.49 is territory where customers demonstrably left.

4.title: Why not touch the trial economics

cells: Falls on free users, not payers

4.notes: Free-plan users generate 58% of our call revenue. The two break-even points rest on an untested assumption about how sign-ups respond to price.

5.title: A push to annual, not a price increase
5.subtitle: Monthly customers leave at 14.9% a month. Annual customers leave at 3.2%.
columns: Worth to us over twelve months
5.notes: Someone who moves to annual is worth more than someone who stays and pays more. The notice must present annual as the obvious cheaper option.

bullets.label: The churn cost
bullets.text: Every estimate compares customers at different price levels today.

bullets.label: Thin margin
bullets.text: One point of extra churn separates 0.70 MSEK from nothing.

bullets.label: They already declined annual
bullets.text: They pay 40% above the advertised price today.

bullets.label: Churn matters more than price
bullets.text: 10% to 8% would beat any change here.

6.title: What we need to find out
bullets: Did revenue actually rise during 2018–20? We judged it a failure on customer numbers alone.
Was the loss really about a third, and over what period?
How much of the 2019 decline was customers moving to the new free plan, not leaving?
Why is the Premium revenue line 50% higher than subscribers times price?
What share of new customers are outside the US buying a US number?
What is churn for monthly US number holders specifically?
6.notes: The first question decides how much weight the 2018–19 story carries. It does not affect the plan change.
